title: Words That Cover Every Letter Demand
statement:
You get two lists of lowercase words, words and demands. A word covers a demand if it contains every letter of the demand at least as many times as the demand does. Order does not matter: "listen" covers "nil", and "tree" covers "ee" but not "eee".

Return every word from words that covers all demands, in the order they appear in words.

examples.why: Together the demands need two n's, an a and a b. "cabana" has only one n.
"tree" has one t, "trot" has no e. Merging the demands into the letter set {t, r, e} and ignoring counts would wrongly accept "tree".
Each demand is checked on its own, so two e's are enough. Adding the demands up (three e's) would reject "seed" too.

hints: Checking each word against each demand works but repeats a lot. Can you merge all the demands into a single requirement first?
A word covers every demand exactly when, for each letter, it has at least the most that any single demand asks for.
Build need[c] = max over demands of count of c. Then each word needs one 26-letter comparison against need.

explain.intuition:
Each demand is a per-letter minimum. Covering all of them at once means meeting the strictest minimum for every letter, and the strictest minimum for a letter is just the largest count any single demand asks for. So fold all demands into one array need[26] by taking per-letter maxima.

Now each word is compared against one combined demand instead of thousands. It is like merging several permission scopes into one before checking each user: you check the union once, not every scope per user. The trap is in how you merge: maximum, not sum and not "letter present".
steps: For every demand, count its letters; update need[c] = max(need[c], count[c]).
For every word, count its letters.
Keep the word if count[c] ≥ need[c] for all 26 letters.
Return the kept words in their original order.
pitfalls: Summing the demands' counts instead of taking the maximum (third example).
Merging demands into a set of letters and ignoring how many times each is needed (second example).
Checking every word against every demand: 10 000 × 10 000 pairs is far too slow.

solutions.title: Check every word against every demand
solutions.idea: Count letters once per word and per demand, then compare each pair.

solutions.title: Merge demands by per-letter maximum
solutions.idea: Fold all demands into one need array of per-letter maxima, then test each word once.

followups: Demands arrive one by one while words stay fixed. How do you keep the answer up to date cheaply?
Letters can be any Unicode character. What replaces the 26-slot arrays?
